title: MongoDB Replication: A Handwritten Deep Dive
summary: Ten dense study-note pages that go from replica set fundamentals to oplog internals, elections, chained replication, and the read preference vs write concern trade-offs, ending with an ops playbook of the mistakes that cause 3 a.m. pages.

chapters.title: Replication 101: Why Copy Your Data
points: Replication = keeping identical copies of your data across several mongod processes; that group is a replica set.
Three wins: high availability (automatic failover), durability (survive disk or node loss), and maintenance with zero downtime.
Anatomy: exactly one PRIMARY accepts all writes; SECONDARY members replicate asynchronously by replaying the primary's oplog.
The oplog is the replication bloodstream: every write is recorded in the primary's oplog, then secondaries pull and apply it.
Failover is automatic: if the primary dies, survivors elect a new primary within seconds and the driver reroutes writes.
Minimum sane topology = 3 data-bearing voting members (P-S-S); a single-node set is for local dev only.
Replication is asynchronous by default: a w:1 ack means 'on the primary', not 'safe on every copy'.
Every member must share the same replica set name (replSet option) to join the group.
Bootstrap: rs.initiate() on the first member, then rs.add('host:port') for each remaining member.
Connect with a seed list or mongodb+srv URI listing several hosts so drivers discover the topology and the new primary.
Cost trade-off: each extra copy multiplies storage and write amplification - replicas are bought, not free.

chapters.title: The Cast: Member Types and When to Use Each
points: PRIMARY: the sole writer; records every change in its oplog; loses the role if it cannot reach a majority.
SECONDARY: read-only data copy that continuously fetches and applies the oplog from its sync source.
ARBITER: votes in elections but stores no data and can never be primary - it exists only to break voting ties.
Priority 0 secondary: priority:0 means never primary - ideal for dedicated reporting or backup nodes.
Hidden member: hidden:true + priority:0 - a data node invisible to driver read routing; almost always combined with priority 0.
Delayed member: secondaryDelaySecs (formerly slaveDelay), e.g. 3600 - a rolling time machine against dropped collections and bad migrations.
Hard limits: at most 7 voting members and 50 total members per replica set.
Non-voting members (votes:0) add data copies beyond the voting cap without changing quorum math.
PSS (primary + 2 secondaries) is the standard; PSA (secondary swapped for an arbiter) is cheaper but creates w:majority availability dilemmas.
Inspect roles with rs.conf(): each members[] entry has host, priority, votes, hidden, secondaryDelaySecs, tags.
Rule of thumb: odd number of data-bearing voting nodes; treat arbiters as a last-resort budget hack.
Geo pattern: a hidden, delayed, priority-0 node in another DC = disaster insurance that never takes traffic.

chapters.title: The Oplog: Your Database's Flight Recorder
points: The oplog (local.oplog.rs) is a capped collection: a fixed-size, rolling log of every data modification on a member.
Every write on the primary appends one oplog entry; secondaries tail this log to build identical copies.
Entry anatomy: ts (timestamp), op (i insert, u update, d delete, c command), ns (db.collection), o (the change document).
Idempotency rule: MongoDB logs the effect, not the intent - an update entry stores the resulting $set-style change so replaying twice is safe.
Ops touching many documents (multi:true updates, big deletes) explode into one oplog entry per document affected.
Default oplog size is about 5% of free disk space, floored at 990 MB on 64-bit Linux; override with replication.oplogSizeMB.
Oplog window = the time span covered from the oldest to the newest entry; secondaries must stay inside it to keep syncing.
Fall outside the window (RECOVERING / stale) and the only cure is a full initial sync - hours of copying on large data sets.
Same size cap, different workloads: a write-heavy hour can shrink the window from days to minutes - size for your busiest hour.
Inspect it: rs.printReplicationInfo() shows log length and window; query local.oplog.rs directly for auditing or CDC.
Change streams are a managed view over the oplog - resume tokens map onto oplog timestamps.
Oplog timestamps double as cluster time, the currency behind causally consistent sessions and majority commit points.

chapters.title: Catching Up: Initial Sync, Lag, Flow Control
points: Initial sync = building a new secondary from scratch: copy all collections from a source, then replay oplog up to the present.
Triggers: adding a member, recovering a stale node, or manually resyncing a damaged one.
After initial sync, the member enters SECONDARY state and streams oplog entries from its sync source with a tailable cursor.
Replication lag = primary's newest oplog time minus a secondary's last applied optime - the number that rules everything.
Measure it: rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo(), or rs.status() comparing members[].optimeDate values.
Lag causes ranked: initial syncs, write bursts exceeding apply capacity, slower secondary disks/CPU, network distance.
Oplog application is multi-threaded: secondaries batch entries and apply them in parallel while honoring write dependencies.
Flow control (4.2+): the primary throttles new writes when majority-commit lag approaches flowControlTargetLagSeconds - lag insurance paid in throughput.
The majority commit point advances as secondaries ack their applied position; it gates w:majority visibility and snapshot reads.
Each oplog entry carries term and wall-clock metadata so a stale primary cannot inject entries into a newer term.
A secondary chained to a lagging sync source inherits that lag - check syncSourceHost when one node trails.
Consequence to internalize: any un-replicated write is exactly one failover away from vanishing.

chapters.title: Elections: How a New Primary Is Chosen
points: Every member heartbeats every other member every 2 seconds - the liveness fabric of the set.
If members hear nothing from the primary for electionTimeoutMillis (default 10000), they conclude it is dead and call an election.
Elections use protocol version 1 (PV1), a Raft-inspired consensus: one primary per term, a majority of votes required.
Candidate checklist: electable (priority > 0), reasonably caught up on the oplog, and able to see a majority of voting members.
Highest priority wins when equally caught up - assign priorities to steer primaries into your best datacenter.
Every election increments the term; a primary that sees a higher term steps down immediately (split-brain protection).
A primary that loses majority visibility self-steps-down - it stops accepting writes rather than fork history.
Typical failover timeline: 10 s timeout + a few seconds of voting + catch-up = roughly 12-15 s without a writable primary.
Catch-up phase: the newly elected primary first pulls missing entries from peers before resuming writes.
Rehearse deliberately: rs.stepDown() demotes the primary and triggers an election - do this in staging regularly.
Even-numbered voting sets without a tie-breaker can deadlock: no candidate can gather a majority.
Post-election surprise: writes acked only by the old primary (w:1) may not exist on the new one - rollbacks happen.

layout.note: Elections - choosing the next primary

chapters.title: Chained Replication: Secondaries Syncing Secondaries
points: Definition: a secondary replicates from another secondary (its sync source) instead of directly from the primary.
Default behavior: each secondary picks the closest member (lowest ping) whose oplog is fresh enough - chains form on their own.
Purpose: spare the primary's network - one copy crosses the WAN, distant nodes then sync from it, not from the primary.
Typical habitat: geo-distributed sets where a region's secondaries would otherwise stream every write across an ocean.
Cost 1: lag compounds hop by hop - every chained link adds its own fetch and apply delay.
Cost 2: the majority commit point advances more slowly, so w:majority writes and snapshot reads get slower too.
Chaining can mask a sick primary: a downstream secondary looks healthy while its degraded sync source holds it back.
Turn it off: rs.reconfig with settings.chainingAllowed: false forces all members to pull straight from the primary.
See who feeds whom: rs.status() -> members[].syncSourceHost shows the current chain.
Observability rule: alert on each member's own applied optime, not the set's average lag - chains hide outliers.
One-line trade-off: chaining trades commit latency and lag visibility for primary bandwidth.

chapters.title: Read Preference: Choosing Where Reads Go
points: Read preference is the driver's routing rule for which member type serves each read.
The five modes: primary (default), primaryPreferred, secondary, secondaryPreferred, nearest.
primary is the only mode that guarantees read-your-own-writes within a logical session.
nearest ignores role entirely - lowest round-trip latency wins, primary included.
secondary and secondaryPreferred offload analytics, dashboards, and search from the write path.
The classic footgun: flipping the app to secondary reads 'for performance', then debugging why users cannot see what they just saved.
maxStalenessSeconds bounds how far behind a secondary may be to still receive reads (minimum 90 seconds).
Tag sets route reads by member tags, e.g. purpose:reporting or dc:eu - pin workloads to specific nodes.
Hidden members are never selected by read preference, regardless of tags.
Transactions require primary read preference - secondaries cannot serve transactional reads.
Set the preference at any scope: connection string (readPreference=secondaryPreferred), database, collection, or single operation.
Decision shortcut: money and checkout paths -> primary; dashboards and search -> secondaryPreferred + maxStalenessSeconds + tags.

chapters.title: Write Concern: When Is a Write 'Written'?
points: Write concern defines how many members must acknowledge a write before it reports success.
w:0 - fire and forget: no ack, fastest, silent data loss on any hiccup; only for lossy telemetry.
w:1 - the old default: primary acks; the write lives on one node until replication catches up.
w:'majority' - a majority of voting data-bearing members applied it; survives single-node failure and elections.
j:true waits for the on-disk journal; since 5.0 journaling is on by default and w:'majority' implies journalled acks.
wtimeout caps the waiting; on timeout inspect writeConcernError - the write may still complete later.
From MongoDB 5.0 the implicit default write concern is w:'majority' (it was w:1 before) - newer apps are safer out of the box.
PSA sets keep w:1 as default because counting members toward majority could stall writes - a deliberate availability trade.
Every step of durability is a step of latency: each additional ack is a network round trip to the farthest required member.
Override granularity: set once per client, then override per database, per collection, or per single operation.
Tag-based custom write concerns (getLastErrorModes) can demand an ack from each datacenter - powerful, rarely used.
Policy of thumb: financial or mutable state -> w:'majority'; high-volume append-only logs -> w:1; never w:0 for data you care about.

layout.note: Write concern - when does a write count?

w:1 + async replication = the write that was there, until failover wasn't

chapters.title: Rollbacks, Read Concern and the Consistency Dial
points: Rollback: a former primary rejoins holding writes the new primary never saw; those writes are ejected from its oplog.
Rolled-back data lands in rollback files under dbPath as BSON - recover manually with bsondump and scripts; there is no auto-merge.
Rollbacks are the punishment for w:1 on writes you needed to keep; w:'majority' writes are rollback-proof.
Read concern local: returns this member's newest data, even data that might later roll back - fastest, weakest.
Read concern majority: returns only data committed at the majority commit point - the natural pair for w:'majority' writes.
Read concern linearizable: strongest single-document read; requires primary read preference and pays a commit-point wait.
Read concern snapshot: a consistent point-in-time view; required for multi-document transactions.
Causally consistent sessions: the client tracks cluster time so a write-then-read stays ordered, even across secondaries.
Retryable writes: drivers transparently retry a write once across network errors and failovers - why well-behaved apps often survive elections silently.
The dial: w:0/j:false -> w:1 -> w:'majority'+j mirrors latency vs safety; benchmark your SLO at each stop.
Cross-region gotcha: majority acks across oceans can add 100 ms+ per write - keep the voting quorum in one region.
Design mantra: choose guarantees per operation class; do not set the strongest combination globally and wonder why p99 doubled.

chapters.title: Ops Playbook: Mistakes, Monitoring, One-Page Recap
points: Mistake: even number of voting members -> some failures leave no majority -> election deadlock; keep voting membership odd.
Mistake: arbiter as the third node to save money -> PSA commit dilemmas; three real data nodes cost less than one data-loss incident.
Mistake: default oplog size on a write-heavy cluster -> secondaries tumble out of the window -> surprise initial syncs.
Mistake: secondary reads 'to scale' without maxStalenessSeconds -> users see yesterday's writes and file tickets.
Mistake: one-host connection string -> after failover the app talks to a secondary forever, or just dies.
Mistake: assuming w:1 is safe 'because we have replicas' - lag means the replicas may not have it yet.
Monitoring basics: rs.status() for member state, lastHeartbeat, pingMs, and optime lag - alert per member, not per set.
Monitoring extras: rs.printReplicationInfo() (oplog window), rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo() (per-node lag), db.hello() for the current primary.
Chaos drill: run rs.stepDown() in staging on a schedule - an app that never survived an election in staging will not survive one in prod.
Cheap insurance: one hidden, delayed, priority-0 member gives you an hour-ago copy after every fat-fingered drop.
Standard topology: PSS across three availability zones, chaining on, w:'majority' defaults, primary reads, tags for reporting nodes.
The recap: primary + oplog + elections move writes; read preference picks who serves reads; write concern decides when a write counts.
